title: "PHP PDO Prepared Statements: Stop SQL Injection in 5 Steps"

categories: ["development", "php"]
primaryCategory: "development"
description: "PHP PDO prepared statements stop SQL injection by design. Learn placeholders, fetch modes, transactions, and how to prove the protection actually works."
focusKeyword: "php pdo prepared statements"
takeaways:
  - "Prepared statements send the query structure to MySQL first, so bound values are treated purely as data."
  - "Set ERRMODE_EXCEPTION, use utf8mb4 in the DSN and turn off emulated prepares so MySQL binds parameters natively."
  - "In the real test, the payload x' OR '1'='1 leaked every row through a concatenated query but returned nothing when prepared."
  - "Wrap multi step writes such as money transfers in a transaction so a failure rolls everything back cleanly."
  - "Table and column names must come from trusted code, and an in memory SQLite database can stand in for MySQL during tests."
image: "/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/php-pdo-prepared-statements.webp"

<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">PHP</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">MySQL</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">PDO</span>
  </div>

  <p class="bx-lede">One unescaped variable dropped into a SQL string is all it takes to hand a stranger read access to an entire database. PHP PDO prepared statements close that door by design, not by remembering to escape every value correctly every single time.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="why-php-pdo-prepared-statements-are-the-safe-default-for-mysql">Why PHP PDO Prepared Statements Are the Safe Default for MySQL</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A raw query built by gluing a variable into a SQL string asks the database to treat user input as part of the command itself. Anything typed into that input becomes something the database will execute.</p>

  <p>A prepared statement changes that relationship entirely. The query structure is sent to MySQL first, compiled, and locked in place. The values arrive afterward, purely as data, with no way to change what the query does.</p>

  <p>That separation is the entire security model. It does not depend on remembering to escape a string correctly, because there is no string concatenation step left to forget. Once PHP PDO prepared statements are the default habit for every query, an entire class of vulnerability simply stops being possible by accident.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p>Set <code>PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE</code> to <code>PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION</code> on every connection. Without it, a failed query just returns false silently instead of throwing something the rest of the code can actually react to.</p>
  </div>

  <p>The <a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet</a> lists parameterized queries as the single most effective primary defense, ahead of input validation or escaping as a first line of protection.</p>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="connecting-to-mysql-with-a-proper-dsn-and-error-mode">Connecting to MySQL With a Proper DSN and Error Mode</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The connection string, called a DSN, tells PDO which driver to use and where to find the server. Getting the character set right here matters more than it looks.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">db_connect.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">$dsn</span> = <span class="tok-str">'mysql:host=127.0.0.1;dbname=app;charset=utf8mb4'</span>;

<span class="tok-val">$pdo</span> = <span class="tok-kw">new</span> PDO(<span class="tok-val">$dsn</span>, <span class="tok-str">'app_user'</span>, <span class="tok-val">$password</span>, [
    PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
    PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
    PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => <span class="tok-val">false</span>,
]);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Setting <code>ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES</code> to false is easy to skip, but it matters. Without it, PDO can quietly build the final query as a string on the PHP side before sending it, which reopens some of the exact risk prepared statements exist to close.</p>

  <p>Turning it off forces MySQL itself to handle the parameter binding natively, which is both the more secure setting and, in most cases, the faster one. PHP's own <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/pdo.setattribute.php" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PDO::setAttribute() manual page</a> lists every driver option available, including the emulation flag used above.</p>

  <p>MySQL's own <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/mysqlnd/en/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">mysqlnd documentation</a> explains why native prepared statement support depends on which underlying driver PHP was built against, which matters if a hosting provider ships an older configuration.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p>SQL injection has its own official classification, <a href="https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CWE-89</a>, in the industry standard list of software weakness types. It has remained one of the most consistently exploited web vulnerabilities for over two decades, largely because the fix is simple but easy to skip under deadline pressure.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="positional-versus-named-placeholders">Positional Versus Named Placeholders</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>PDO supports two placeholder styles, and mixing them in the same query is not allowed. Picking one deliberately, rather than whichever comes to mind first, keeps a query easier to read later.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">placeholders.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-cm">// positional placeholders, values passed in order</span>
<span class="tok-val">$stmt</span> = <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = ? AND total > ?'</span>);
<span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->execute([<span class="tok-str">'shipped'</span>, <span class="tok-val">100</span>]);

<span class="tok-cm">// named placeholders, order does not matter</span>
<span class="tok-val">$stmt</span> = <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = :status AND total > :total'</span>);
<span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->execute([<span class="tok-str">'status'</span> => <span class="tok-str">'shipped'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'total'</span> => <span class="tok-val">100</span>]);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Positional placeholders read cleanly for a short query with one or two values. Named placeholders scale better once a query grows past three or four parameters, since the array keys document what each value actually means.</p>

  <p>Everything covered in these PHP PDO prepared statements examples works identically against <a href="https://mariadb.org/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MariaDB</a> too, since it speaks the same wire protocol and PDO driver as MySQL itself.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p>Never build a placeholder name from user input, even indirectly. Only the values bound to <code>:status</code> or <code>?</code> are safe from injection, the query structure itself, including which columns and tables are named, always has to come from code the application controls.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="proving-prepared-statements-actually-stop-injection">Proving Prepared Statements Actually Stop Injection</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>It is one thing to be told prepared statements are safe. It is more convincing to actually feed a classic injection payload to both a raw concatenated query and a prepared one, side by side, and watch what each one does with it.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">injection_test.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">find_user_unsafe</span>(PDO <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>, <span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$username</span>): <span class="tok-kw">array</span> {
    <span class="tok-cm">// never do this: raw string concatenation, shown only to prove the point</span>
    <span class="tok-val">$sql</span> = <span class="tok-str">"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '$username'"</span>;
    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->query(<span class="tok-val">$sql</span>)->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC);
}

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">find_user_safe</span>(PDO <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>, <span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$username</span>): <span class="tok-kw">array</span> {
    <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span> = <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = :username'</span>);
    <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->execute([<span class="tok-str">'username'</span> => <span class="tok-val">$username</span>]);
    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">$stmt</span>->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC);
}

<span class="tok-val">$payload</span> = <span class="tok-str">"x' OR '1'='1"</span>;</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>That payload is the textbook example for a reason: against a raw concatenated query, it turns a search for one specific username into a condition that matches every row in the table instead.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output comparing an unsafe concatenated query, which leaks every user row when given a classic OR 1=1 SQL injection payload, against a safe prepared statement, which correctly returns zero rows" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from running the same malicious input against both versions of the query.</p>

  <p>The unsafe version leaks every row in the table. The prepared statement version returns nothing, because MySQL never interprets the payload as anything other than the literal text of a username that does not exist.</p>

  <p>Injection remains listed in <a href="https://owasp.org/Top10/A03_2021-Injection/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OWASP's Top 10</a> as one of the most common and most preventable web application risks, largely for exactly this reason.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="choosing-a-fetch-mode-that-matches-what-comes-next">Choosing a Fetch Mode That Matches What Comes Next</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>PDO can hand back a result row shaped several different ways, and picking the wrong one usually just means extra conversion code later rather than any real bug.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Fetch Mode</th><th>Shape Returned</th><th>Good For</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>FETCH_ASSOC</td><td>Associative array, column name keys</td><td>General purpose, the most common default</td></tr>
        <tr><td>FETCH_OBJ</td><td>Plain stdClass object</td><td>Quick property access without a defined class</td></tr>
        <tr><td>FETCH_CLASS</td><td>Instance of a named class</td><td>Mapping a row directly onto a domain object</td></tr>
        <tr><td>FETCH_COLUMN</td><td>A single scalar value</td><td>Counts, existence checks, one column lookups</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>Setting <code>PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE</code> once at connection time, the way the earlier connection example does, means every later call to <code>fetch()</code> or <code>fetchAll()</code> behaves consistently without repeating the mode argument everywhere it is called.</p>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="wrapping-multi-step-writes-in-a-transaction">Wrapping Multi Step Writes in a Transaction</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Some operations only make sense as a single atomic unit. Moving money between two accounts is the classic example: either both balances update, or neither does.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">transaction_test.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">transfer</span>(PDO <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>, <span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$from</span>, <span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$to</span>, <span class="tok-kw">int</span> <span class="tok-val">$amount</span>): <span class="tok-kw">void</span> {
    <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->beginTransaction();

    <span class="tok-kw">try</span> {
        <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE name = :name'</span>)
            ->execute([<span class="tok-str">'amt'</span> => <span class="tok-val">$amount</span>, <span class="tok-str">'name'</span> => <span class="tok-val">$from</span>]);

        <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->prepare(<span class="tok-str">'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + :amt WHERE name = :name'</span>)
            ->execute([<span class="tok-str">'amt'</span> => <span class="tok-val">$amount</span>, <span class="tok-str">'name'</span> => <span class="tok-val">$to</span>]);

        <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->commit();
    } <span class="tok-kw">catch</span> (Exception <span class="tok-val">$e</span>) {
        <span class="tok-val">$pdo</span>->rollBack();
        <span class="tok-kw">throw</span> <span class="tok-val">$e</span>;
    }
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Simulating a failure partway through the transfer, after the first update has already run but before the second one does, shows exactly what the rollback is protecting against.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output showing account balances before a transfer, a simulated failure partway through the transfer, and the balances confirmed unchanged after the transaction rolled back" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from a transfer that fails partway through and rolls back cleanly.</p>

  <p>Without the transaction wrapping both statements, that same failure would have left one account debited with no matching credit ever applied, a half finished write with no way to tell it happened at all.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="handling-errors-without-leaking-database-details">Handling Errors Without Leaking Database Details</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>With <code>ERRMODE_EXCEPTION</code> set, a failed query throws a <code>PDOException</code> instead of returning false silently. That exception often carries the exact table and column names involved, which is exactly the kind of detail that should never reach a user facing response, even in an application already built around PHP PDO prepared statements throughout.</p>

  <p>Catching it, logging the full detail internally, and returning a generic message to the caller follows the same principle covered in <a href="/rest-api-in-php-without-a-framework/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">building a REST API in PHP without a framework</a>, where a consistent JSON error shape never exposes internal exception messages directly.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Always use PHP PDO prepared statements for values:</b> the query structure comes from code, the values come from a bound parameter, never a concatenated string.</li>
    <li><b>Disable emulated prepares:</b> lets MySQL itself handle the parameter binding natively instead of PHP building the final string beforehand.</li>
    <li><b>Set a real error mode:</b> a silent false on failure is far easier to miss than a thrown exception.</li>
    <li><b>Wrap related writes in a transaction:</b> a multi step update should never be allowed to finish only halfway.</li>
    <li><b>Never log full exception details to the user:</b> internal logs can hold the detail, the response back to the caller should not.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">08</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="testing-query-code-without-a-live-mysql-server">Testing Query Code Without a Live MySQL Server</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>PDO speaks the same interface regardless of which database driver sits behind it. Swapping the DSN for <code>sqlite::memory:</code> during a test run creates a real, disposable database in memory that behaves identically for prepared statement mechanics.</p>

  <p>Every real output shown in this article, including the injection test and the transaction rollback, was produced exactly this way: real PDO code, executed for real, just against a fast in memory database instead of a network connection to MySQL. <a href="https://phpdelusions.net/pdo" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PHP Delusions' PDO tutorial</a> is one of the most thorough independent references on this exact topic, worth reading after this article for the deeper edge cases.</p>

  <p>Input that eventually reaches one of these queries should already have passed through the same kind of checks covered in <a href="/validating-and-sanitizing-user-input-in-php-forms/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">validating and sanitizing user input in PHP forms</a>. A prepared statement stops injection, but it will still happily store a value that is simply wrong.</p>

  <p>A scheduled task that runs these same queries repeatedly, the way the <a href="/php-cron-jobs/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">PHP cron jobs</a> article covers, benefits from the exact connection and fetch mode setup shown here too, and a long running script that reads the same reference data over and over is often a good candidate for the <a href="/caching-database-queries-in-php-with-redis/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">caching database queries in PHP with Redis</a> pattern covered elsewhere in this series.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p><a href="https://www.sqlite.org/mostdeployed.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SQLite</a> is reportedly the most widely deployed database engine in the world by install count, largely because it ships inside phones, browsers, and countless applications as an embedded library rather than a separate server.</p>
  </div>

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>Are PHP PDO prepared statements enough on their own to stop SQL injection?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, for the values bound as parameters. The query structure itself, including table and column names, still has to come from trusted code rather than user input.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>Should positional or named placeholders be used by default?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Either works safely. Named placeholders tend to read more clearly once a query has more than a few parameters, since each key documents what the value represents.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>What does disabling emulated prepares actually change?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>It forces MySQL to handle parameter binding natively instead of PHP assembling the final query string beforehand, which is both more secure and typically faster.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>Why wrap related writes in a transaction instead of running them separately?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Without a transaction, a failure partway through a multi step update can leave the data in a half finished state with no clean way to tell it happened.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>Can PDO code be tested without a live MySQL server running?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes. Swapping the DSN for an in memory SQLite database gives a real, fast database for tests, since PDO's prepared statement behavior is consistent across drivers.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>PHP PDO prepared statements separate data from structure</h4><p>The query compiles before any value ever arrives.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>Placeholders come in two styles</h4><p>Named placeholders scale better once a query has several values.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>Emulated prepares should be off</h4><p>Letting MySQL bind parameters natively is safer and usually faster.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Fetch mode shapes the result</h4><p>Pick the mode that matches what the calling code actually needs.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Transactions protect multi step writes</h4><p>A partial failure should never leave data half updated.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>SQLite can stand in for tests</h4><p>Swapping the DSN gives a real database without a live server.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
